name: INA199A1DCKR
title: 26 V bidirectional zero-drift current-shunt monitor, INA199 series
summary: The INA199 is a voltage-output current-sense amplifier that reads the drop across a shunt with the shunt at –0.3 V to 26 V of common mode, on either the high or the low side, independent of its own 2.7 V to 26 V supply. A zero-drift input keeps offset under 150 µV, so full-scale shunt drops near 10 mV work. Gain is fixed at 50, 100 or 200 V/V, and a REF pin places the zero-current output anywhere from 0 V to V+ for one- or two-way measurement. It draws at most 100 µA and comes in SC70-6 and UQFN-10.

circuits.title: Simplified schematic
circuits.description: The shunt sits in the supply line to the load, IN+ on its supply side and IN– on its load side, at any common mode from –0.3 V to 26 V. V+ takes 2.7 V to 26 V with a 0.01 µF to 0.1 µF bypass to ground. REF goes either to a reference voltage or to ground; OUT is the output.

circuits.title: Typical application
circuits.description: A high-side shunt between a power supply and a grounded load, read by a microcontroller's ADC. The INA199 runs from 5 V with a 0.1 µF bypass, REF is grounded so the output sits at 0 V for no current and rises with current toward the load.

circuits.title: Filter at input pins
circuits.description: A differential low-pass ahead of the inputs: a series resistor under 10 Ω from each end of the shunt and CF across IN+ and IN–. The resistors meet the part's internal input resistance and bias network, which adds gain error (see the gain error factor). V+ comes from a separate power supply with a 0.1 µF bypass.

circuits.title: Shutdown by switching the supply
circuits.description: The part has no shutdown pin, so V+ is fed by a logic gate or transistor switch, itself driven by a shutdown control line. With V+ off, each input still sees just over 1 MΩ (the 1 MΩ feedback resistor plus R3 or R4) to OUT and to REF; REF goes to a reference voltage, directly or through a buffer amplifier, or to ground.
notes: R3 and R4 are 20 kΩ (INA199x1), 10 kΩ (INA199x2) or 5 kΩ (INA199x3).

circuits.title: Differential sensing to cancel REF impedance
circuits.description: REF is set by a resistor divider from the supply line to ground, and the ADC reads OUT against the REF node rather than against ground, so the divider's impedance at REF drops out of the result. V+ takes 2.7 V to 26 V with a 0.01 µF to 0.1 µF bypass.

circuits.title: Transient protection with two Zener diodes
circuits.description: For common-mode transients above 26 V: a 10 Ω resistor from each end of the shunt to its input, and a Zener from each input to ground. The resistors give the Zeners a working impedance; supply switching and REF are as in the shutdown circuit.

circuits.title: Transient protection with one transzorb and input clamps
circuits.description: For transients too energetic for small Zeners: one transzorb from the IN+ node to ground and two diodes in antiparallel across IN+ and IN–, after 10 Ω resistors from each end of the shunt. Supply switching and REF are as in the shutdown circuit.
notes: D2 and D3 can be one dual series diode in SOT-523 or SOD-523.

circuits.title: Transient protection with ferrite beads
circuits.description: Against fast input transients (over 2 kV/µs) that can damage version A parts: a ferrite bead from each end of the shunt to its input and a 0.01 µF to 0.1 µF capacitor from each input to ground. V+ takes 2.7 V to 26 V with its own 0.01 µF to 0.1 µF bypass; REF goes to a reference voltage or to ground.

circuits.title: Unidirectional operation
circuits.description: REF is grounded, so the output rests at ground with no current and rises for current from the bus supply to the load; it cannot go below ground for current the other way. V+ comes from a separate power supply with a 0.1 µF bypass.

circuits.title: Bidirectional operation
circuits.description: The voltage on REF sets the output for zero current; the output moves above it for current toward the load and below it for current the other way. A switch takes REF either straight to a reference voltage or to an op-amp follower driven from a two-resistor divider of that reference to ground. V+ comes from a separate power supply with a 0.1 µF bypass.

equations.name: Gain error factor
equations.expr: Gain Error Factor = (1250 × RINT) / ((1250 × RS) + (1250 × RINT) + (RS × RINT))

where.RINT: internal input resistor, R3 and R4 (20 kΩ, 10 kΩ or 5 kΩ by gain)
where.RS: external resistance in series with each input

equations.note: The share of the shunt voltage that reaches the input pins when series resistors are added; the device gain error factor table gives it reduced for each gain.

equations.name: Gain error from series resistance

where.Gain Error Factor: from the equation above or the device gain error factor table

equations.note: With 10 Ω in series with each input: INA199x2 gives a factor of 0.991 and about 0.89 % gain error; INA199x1 gives 0.991 and 0.84 %.

operation.text: Gain is fixed inside the part: 50 V/V for INA199x1, 100 V/V for x2, 200 V/V for x3. Versions A, B and C differ in the lowest input common mode (–0.3 V for A, –0.1 V for B and C), in HBM ESD rating (±2000 V for A, ±3500 V for B and C), in maximum gain error over temperature (±1.5 % for A and B, ±1 % for C), and in transient robustness. An automotive-qualified version, INA199-Q1, exists.

The inputs read the shunt anywhere from –0.3 V (version A) to 26 V of common mode, regardless of the 2.7 V to 26 V supply; the zero-drift input stage keeps offset at or below 150 µV with no more than 0.5 µV/°C drift from –40 °C to 125 °C. The inputs tolerate the full 26 V whether or not the part is powered; the output can only swing within the supply.

The low offset lets the full-scale shunt drop be about 10 mV where amplifiers without zero drift usually need about 100 mV, cutting shunt dissipation by roughly ten. Or the low gains can take larger drops for wide dynamic range: an INA199A1 on 3.3 V handles a 60 mV full-scale drop with only 150 µV of offset.

Run IN+ and IN– to the shunt with as little extra resistance in series with it as possible. A bypass capacitor at the supply pins is needed for stability; noisy or high-impedance supplies may need more decoupling. In the RSW package each input has two pins, and both pins of an input are tied together.

Filtering at OUT would throw away the internal buffer's low output impedance, so filtering goes at the inputs, with the internal resistances' ±30 % tolerance in mind. Keep each series resistor at 10 Ω or below. With a differential voltage applied the internal bias network draws unequal currents into the two inputs; through external series resistors that mismatch turns into a differential error that reduces the voltage seen at the pins, which appears as gain error.

There is no shutdown pin; the supply current is low enough that a logic gate output or a transistor switch can feed V+ directly. Unpowered, each input sees slightly over 1 MΩ to OUT and to REF. The current through the REF path depends on what drives REF (ground, a live reference, or an unpowered source that may be open); an unpowered INA199 output conducts well to ground, so the current into OUT is the shunt common mode across about 1 MΩ. Powered, each input also draws an almost constant, well-matched 25 µA while the common mode is 3 V or more; below 2 V only the 1 MΩ paths matter.

Impedance at REF degrades common-mode rejection, as in any difference amplifier. Driving REF straight from a reference or supply is fine; a resistor divider on REF needs an op-amp buffer. Where the output is read differentially (a differential ADC, or two ADC inputs), measuring OUT against REF cancels the effect.

Only Zener diodes or Zener-type transient absorbers (transzorbs) are fast enough; other absorbers respond too slowly. Add a resistor from each shunt end to its input as the Zener's working impedance, usually about 10 Ω; larger values add gain error. For short transients, 10 Ω with the smallest low-power Zeners (SOT-523 or SOD-523) takes the least space. Where more absorption is needed, fit a single transzorb plus two antiparallel diodes between the inputs, such as a dual series diode in SOT-523 or SOD-523. Either way the INA199 and its protection take less board area than an SO-8.

Input transients above 2 kV/µs can latch the input ESD structures of version A parts to ground, and the shunt current then destroys the die. A filter ahead of the inputs prevents it: ferrite beads under 10 Ω at dc and over 600 Ω at 100 MHz to 200 MHz, with 0.01 µF to 0.1 µF capacitors, keeping series resistance under 10 Ω for accuracy. Versions B and C use ESD structures that cannot latch this way and need no such filter.

With REF at ground, zero current gives an output at ground and rising current a rising output. Because the output cannot reach right down to ground, measuring very small currents calls for biasing REF above 50 mV; buffer whatever drives REF to limit common-mode error. REF can instead go to V+: the output then rests 200 mV below the supply and moves down only for negative sense voltage. REF must never be above the supply.

The voltage on REF, anywhere from 0 V to V+, is the output for zero current; positive sense voltage (IN+ above IN–) drives the output above it and negative below it. Mid-supply gives equal range both ways; another level suits currents that are not symmetric.

Connect the inputs to the shunt by a Kelvin (four-wire) connection so that only the shunt's own resistance lies between them; any high-current copper in that path adds large error with a low-value shunt. Place the 0.1 µF supply bypass right at the V+ and GND pins; extra capacitance helps where the supply is noisy or of high impedance.

DCK (SC70-6): body dimensions exclude mold flash and protrusion, which can add up to 0.15 mm per side; it is a JEDEC MO-203 AB outline. RSW (UQFN-10): meets JEDEC MO-288 variation UDEE except for its lower minimum height; nominal body 1.80 mm × 1.40 mm, 0.55 mm maximum height.
